Empirical Research Plan – Medicare’s Supply-Side Effects on Hospitals  
  
================================================================  
1. Identification Strategy  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
Strategy: Difference-in-Differences with Continuous (“dose–response”) Treatment, supplemented by an event-study.  

Why it fits:  
• The policy arrives sharply and nationally on 1 July 1966, giving a clean pre/post break.  
• Ex-ante heterogeneity in private coverage across 11 census sub-regions creates cross-sectional variation in the size of the insurance shock.  
• Hospital outcomes are observed annually for 18 years pre (1948-65) and 9 years post (1966-75), allowing comparison of trends.  
• Hospitals cannot self-select into treatment intensity; pre-1966 coverage was driven by Blue-Cross penetration decades earlier, not by contemporaneous hospital behavior.  

Hence a DID of the form  
Y_hrt = α + θ_r + λ_t + β (Post_t × UninsuredShare_r,1963) + ε_hrt  
yields the causal semi-elasticity “per-ppt increase in insurance coverage.”  
An event study (year-by-year interactions) visualizes dynamics and pre-trends.  
  
2. Treatment and Control  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
Treatment variable: Baseline share of the elderly in the sub-region that were uninsured in 1963: TREAT_r ≡ (1 – PrivateCoverageRate_r,1963). It ranges from 0.49 (New England) to 0.88 (East South Central).  

Control group: Hospitals located in high-previous-coverage regions (low TREAT_r) – effectively the lower quartile of TREAT. They experience only a small insurance shock and serve as the counterfactual trend.  

Timing:  
• Pre-period = 1948–1965 (we exclude 1954 because it is missing).  
• Post-period = 1966–1975.  
We will test robustness to starting post in 1967 to guard against implementation lags.  

No running variable or cutoff is needed (not an RDD).  
  
3. Key Identifying Assumptions  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
A1. Parallel trends: In absence of Medicare, outcomes in high- and low-coverage regions would have evolved in parallel. Plausibility: From 1948–65 there was no nationwide elderly-specific program; Blue-Cross diffusion largely stabilized by the late 1950s. We will check via event-study coefficients for the years –10…–2.  

A2. No differential contemporaneous shocks correlated with TREAT_r that start in 1966. Plausibility: Other Great-Society programs (e.g., Medicaid, War on Poverty) either apply to all regions similarly or target the poor rather than the elderly; nevertheless we will control for time-varying regional income, demographics, and crime.  

A3. Stable unit composition: Hospital openings/closures are not systematically related to TREAT_r around 1966. We can test by estimating DID on an indicator “hospital alive in year t” and by re-running all results on a balanced panel.  

A4. No spillovers across regions: Medicare is national, but the intensity shock comes solely from elderly coverage gaps. Elderly do not relocate en masse in response to eligibility, so cross-region spillovers are minimal.  
  
4. Main Threats & Mitigations  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
Threat 1 – Pre-trend divergence.  
• Mitigation: Display event-study plot; formally test that β_k (k = –10 … –2) jointly equal zero.  
• Add sub-region-specific linear trends; show that β is stable.  

Threat 2 – Other concurrent policies with region-specific bite (e.g., Medicaid, hospital construction grants).  
• Mitigation: Control for state-level Medicaid generosity interacted with Post.  
• Add controls for Hill-Burton hospital construction grants (available annually).  
• Re-estimate after dropping the five states with highest Medicaid per-capita spending in 1967.  

Threat 3 – Endogenous hospital coding / accounting after cost-plus reimbursement (“reasonable costs”).  
• Mitigation: Focus on physical quantities (beds, admissions, technologies) in addition to monetary spending.  
• Show that non-discretionary inputs (e.g., number of operating rooms) respond similarly, which cannot be “book-keeping.”  
  
5. R Code Outline  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
```r
# 0. Packages -----------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)   # fast data wrangling
library(fixest)       # high-dimensional fixed effects
library(ggplot2)

# 1. Load Data ----------------------------------------------------
aha   <- fread("AHA_hospital_1948_1975.csv")           # hospital-level panel
cover <- fread("ElderlyCoverage1963_bySubregion.csv")  # 11 rows
state <- fread("StateControls_1948_1975.csv")          # income, pop, etc.

# 2. Merge & Construct Variables ---------------------------------
aha   <- merge(aha, cover,  by = "subregion")          # adds UninsuredShare63
aha   <- merge(aha, state,  by = c("state","year"))

aha[, post := as.integer(year >= 1966)]
aha[, treat_intensity := UninsuredShare63]             # 0.49–0.88

# Outcomes (examples)
aha[, ln_spend  := log(total_expenditures_1960$)]
aha[, ln_admits := log(inpatient_admissions)]
aha[, tech_OHS  := open_heart_surgery_facility]        # 0/1

# 3. Main DID Specification --------------------------------------
fe_formula <- ln_spend ~ post * treat_intensity +       # key interaction
                          lnincome_state +              # controls
                          violentcrime_state + 
                          infantmort_state | 
                          hospital_id + year

did_main <- feols(fe_formula, data = aha, cluster = ~subregion)
summary(did_main)

# 4. Event-Study --------------------------------------------------
for (yr in 1958:1975){
  aha[, paste0("event_", yr) := as.integer(year == yr) * treat_intensity]
}
event_vars <- grep("^event_", names(aha), value = TRUE)
event_formula <- reformulate(c(event_vars, "lnincome_state",
                               "violentcrime_state", "infantmort_state"),
                             response = "ln_spend")

event_mod <- feols(event_formula, 
                   data = aha[year %between% c(1958,1975)],
                   fixef = ~hospital_id + year,
                   cluster = ~subregion)

# Plot coefficients (omit 1965 as baseline)
coef_df <- data.frame(year = 1958:1975,
                      beta = coef(event_mod)[event_vars],
                      se   = se(event_mod)[event_vars])
coef_df <- coef_df[coef_df$year != 1965,]

ggplot(coef_df, aes(x = year, y = beta)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = beta - 1.96*se, ymax = beta + 1.96*se)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1966, linetype = "dashed") +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Event-study: log spending × uninsured share",
       y = "β_k", x = "Year")

# 5. Robustness Check: Balanced Panel ----------------------------
balanced_ids <- aha[, .N, by = hospital_id][N == length(unique(aha$year)), hospital_id]
did_balanced <- feols(fe_formula, data = aha[hospital_id %in% balanced_ids],
                      cluster = ~subregion)
summary(did_balanced)
```

6. Expected Results  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
Direction: β > 0. Hospitals in areas with larger insurance shocks should expand spending, inputs, and technology adoption.  

Back-of-the-envelope: A 75 p.p. coverage jump (national average) could plausibly raise real hospital spending by 15–20 percent in fully exposed regions. Thus β̂ ≈ 0.20 / 0.75 ≈ 0.27 log-points per 100 p.p., i.e., ≈ 0.0027 per 1 p.p. rise in coverage.  

Capital inputs (beds, equipment) should respond more slowly but still positively; technology indicators may rise by 3–8 p.p. in low-coverage regions relative to high-coverage regions by 1975.  
  
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DID)  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
C1: No pre-trend (parallel trends) ............................. 1  
C2: No differential shocks other than treatment ................ 0.5  
C3: No anticipation (policy unexpected) ........................ 1  
C4: Stable composition of units ................................ 0.5  
C5: No spillovers/interference ................................. 0.5  
TOTAL (out of 5) ............................................... 3.5  
  
Overall, the design is credible but hinges on showing parallel trends and ruling out contemporaneous regional shocks.
